correctness.rationale: For \(e_k(t)=t^{k\alpha}/\Gamma(1+k\alpha)\), the Caputo–Volterra identity \(\mathcal I^\alpha e_k=e_{k+1}\) gives \(x_1=x_0[\beta(N-2I_0)/N-\gamma]\). On \(x_1=0\), \(i_1=(\beta/N)I_0^2>0\), \(x_2=-(\beta/N)i_1[\gamma(N-I_0)+H_2x_0]<0\), and \(x_3=(\beta/N)\gamma i_1x_0(H_3-H_2)>0\), since \(H_3/H_2=\Gamma(1+3\alpha)\Gamma(1+\alpha)/\Gamma(1+2\alpha)^2>1\) by strict Gamma log-convexity. Each admissible incidence has first exponent \(\alpha\) (generic) or \(2\alpha\) (critical). Distinct generic/critical orders could match it only with \(\alpha_{generic}=2\alpha_{critical}\); the nonzero critical \(t^{3\alpha_{critical}}\) term contradicts generic powers in multiples of \(2\alpha_{critical}\). Same-class equality gives equal orders. The proof includes \(\alpha=1\). A standalone finite checker passed 500 critical cases and the exact half-order example; these tests are not the universal proof.

value.rationale: The exceptional hypersurface arises exactly when the leading fractional incidence coefficient vanishes and is identified as a missing natural case of a directly relevant identifiability proposition. A first exponent \(t^{2\alpha}\) can masquerade as the generic order \(2\alpha\); the nonzero next exponent \(t^{3\alpha}\) supplies a definitive mathematical discriminator. This includes a concrete \(\alpha=1/2\) example where the first observed change is linear, but the next term has a fractional power. The opposite signs of early incidence and prevalence changes add epidemiological interpretation. The result is an exact-data structural benchmark, not an empirical performance claim.
